title: U.S. public concern about data centers shifts from unfamiliarity toward local infrastructure burden
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of U.S. adults, July 20-August 9, 2026

mostly_bad_impacts.value: Environment: 39% in January to 54% in August; home energy costs: 38% to 50%; nearby quality of life: 30% to 49%; local jobs: 15% to 24%; local tax revenue: 12% to 21%
mostly_bad_impacts.unit: percent saying data centers have mostly bad impact

local_siting_comfort.value: 60% are not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area; 19% are somewhat comfortable and 7% are extremely or very comfortable

awareness.value: 35% had heard a lot about data centers in August, up from 25% in January; 88% had heard at least a little by August

rural_and_partisan_examples.value: Among rural adults, saying the environmental impact is mostly bad rose from 32% to 50%; among Republicans, saying nearby quality of life is mostly bad rose from 24% to 42%

observations.method: Repeated national survey measures of perceived data-center effects, comfort with local siting, and awareness, with subgroup comparisons by community type and party identification.
observations.uncertainty: The source measures public perceptions and awareness rather than verified local environmental, energy, employment, or tax effects. January-August changes are descriptive and may reflect news coverage, local controversies, or changing question context; the survey does not establish whether concern causes opposition or siting outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, including rural and urban/suburban community types and Republican/Democratic identifiers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising concern may represent improved awareness of a new infrastructure category rather than durable anti-data-center sentiment. Some respondents may distinguish between national AI benefits and local siting costs, and perceived job or tax benefits could still matter even when environmental or quality-of-life concerns rise.

boundary: This record adds a public-legitimacy and local-siting layer to the AI infrastructure trend. It does not infer actual data-center externalities, protest behavior, permitting outcomes, or a causal relationship between awareness and opposition.
